prompt: In a legacy BIOS boot, what is the exact byte value at offset 510 of a valid boot sector, and at offset 511?
choices: 0xAA at offset 510, 0x55 at offset 511
0x55 at offset 510, 0xAA at offset 511
0x55 at both offsets 510 and 511
0x00 at offset 510, 0xFF at offset 511

prompt: In the boot sector source shown in this lesson, the code and message together total exactly 61 bytes before the `times` line. How many padding bytes does `times 510 - ($ - $$) db 0` emit, and why is the target 510 rather than 512?
choices: 451 bytes, because 512 minus 61 equals 451
449 bytes, because the last 2 of the 512 total bytes are reserved for the 0xAA55 signature
510 bytes, because $$ always evaluates to zero
61 bytes, matching the code size exactly

prompt: Why does a POST failure typically get reported as a PC-speaker beep code instead of an on-screen error message?
choices: Beep codes are faster to transmit over the motherboard's control bus than text
Video output is one of the subsystems POST is still testing, and might itself be the failed component, whereas the PC speaker driven by the PIT has no such dependency
On-screen text requires a bootloader to already be loaded, which hasn't happened yet at POST time
Beep codes were an early UEFI feature that BIOS later adopted for consistency

prompt: Under legacy BIOS boot, once BIOS finds a valid boot signature and jumps to 0x7C00, which of the following is true?
choices: BIOS continues supervising the boot process, loading the kernel itself once the bootloader signals it's ready
BIOS's job on that boot is finished; reading a partition table, loading further sectors, and switching CPU modes are entirely the bootloader's responsibility
BIOS switches the CPU into protected mode automatically before jumping, so the bootloader never runs in real mode
BIOS re-checks the 0xAA55 signature after every additional sector the bootloader loads

prompt: A real-mode boot sector is loaded with segment DS = 0x0000. Using segment:offset addressing (physical = segment × 16 + offset), what physical address does DS:0x0010 resolve to if, instead, DS were set to 0x07C0?
Why can't an x86-64 CPU jump directly from 16-bit real mode into 64-bit long mode in a single step?
choices: Long mode requires paging to already be active, and setting up that paging (via CR4.PAE, CR3, and the GDT-based segment mechanism) depends on machinery that only exists once protected mode has been entered first
Intel and AMD deliberately disabled the direct transition in microcode to force compatibility testing
Real mode code cannot execute the `rdmsr`/`wrmsr` instructions needed to read the EFER register under any circumstances
Long mode does not use segment registers at all, so there is nothing for real mode's segments to transition into

prompt: Setting bit 0 of which control register is what actually enables protected mode on x86?
choices: CR2
CR3
CR0
CR4

prompt: What concretely distinguishes booting via UEFI from booting via legacy BIOS, in terms of CPU state handed to the bootloader?
choices: UEFI requires the bootloader to still perform the real-mode-to-long-mode transition itself, exactly like legacy BIOS
On x86-64, UEFI hands off to the bootloader with the CPU already in long mode with paging enabled, while legacy BIOS hands off a CPU still in 16-bit real mode
UEFI does not use a CPU reset vector, so POST never runs under UEFI
Legacy BIOS boots directly into long mode, while UEFI boots into real mode for compatibility with older PE binaries
